ellen-craft.excerpt: In December 1848, an enslaved woman travelled a thousand miles disguised as a white slaveholder, with her husband posing as her slave.
sections: Macon, Georgia

Ellen Craft was born in 1826 in Clinton, Georgia, the daughter of a white slaveholder and an enslaved woman. She looked white, which so angered her father's wife that Ellen was given away to a half-sister in Macon. William Craft was born around 1824 and enslaved in Macon too; at sixteen his family was split up and sold to pay his enslaver's debts. He was apprenticed to a cabinet maker.
The two met in Macon and married; the details, as History.com puts it, remain unknown. They judged escape from Georgia almost impossible. Then William had an idea.
The disguise

Ellen would travel as a sick young white planter going north for treatment, and William as the slave who waited on him. Ellen doubted she could pass, but agreed. William bought the pieces of the disguise in different shops around town so that no one would guess. Ellen, a seamstress, sewed what she could herself.

She cut her hair, and wore a top hat and green spectacles. Bandages round her face suggested illness and hid a face with no beard. Her right arm went into a sling: neither of them could write, and a traveller would be asked to sign for himself. And since a planter would be expected to talk, Ellen would be hard of hearing. Each of them got a few days off before Christmas.
A thousand miles

They left Macon on 21 December 1848 by train for Savannah, 200 miles away, as "Mr William Johnson" and his slave. On the train a Mr Cray, a friend of Ellen's enslaver, sat down beside her; her deafness saved her. From Savannah a steamer took them to Charleston, where a slave dealer at breakfast tried to buy William, and at the ticket office a clerk demanded that "Mr Johnson" sign; another passenger signed for the invalid. On they went, by steamer to Wilmington, by train through Richmond and Fredericksburg, by steamer to Washington, by train to Baltimore.

In Baltimore, on Christmas Eve, an officer stopped William and demanded proof that he belonged to the man he was with, and told Ellen she would have to post a bond. The conductor of their last train confirmed they had been his passengers, the departure bell rang, and the officer let them board. On Christmas morning 1848 they saw the lights of Philadelphia. "A thousand miles" is the title they later gave the journey, an approximation rather than a measured distance. Sources differ on the day they set out, between 18 and 24 December.
Boston, and the slave catchers

In Philadelphia, abolitionists took them in, and a Quaker family in Bucks County taught them to read and write; by the time they left for Boston, three weeks later, they could sign their names. In Boston they lodged with Lewis and Harriet Hayden, William worked as a cabinet maker and Ellen as a seamstress, and they spoke at anti-slavery meetings across New England alongside William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass.

In September 1850 Congress passed the Fugitive Slave Act, and in October two men from Macon, Willis Hughes and John Knight, arrived in Boston with a warrant for the Crafts. The Boston Vigilance Committee hid Ellen in a series of houses, had the two men arrested repeatedly on local charges, and surrounded their hotel with crowds. William armed himself; a newspaper reported about 200 Black Bostonians guarding him. On 1 November the slave catchers left Boston without their prisoners. A week later the Crafts remarried under the laws of a free state, and the minister, Theodore Parker, gave William a revolver.
England, and home

The Crafts sailed for England, where they studied and then taught at the Ockham School in Surrey, raised five children, and in 1860 published their own account, Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom. In 1852 Ellen answered rumours that she wanted to return to slavery with an open letter in the anti-slavery press: she would, she wrote, much rather starve in England a free woman.

After nearly twenty years they came back, and in 1873 opened the Woodville Co-operative Farm School in Bryan County, Georgia, to teach and employ newly freed people. Accusations that William had misused donations led him to sue for libel in 1878; he lost, and the school closed soon after for lack of money. In 1890 they moved to Charleston to live with their daughter. Ellen Craft died in 1891, William in 1900. Several details repeated elsewhere, a line Ellen is said to have spoken on arrival, a stay at the best hotel in Charleston, a first-class carriage, rest on a single source each and are not included here.

garrett-morgan.excerpt: He walked into a gas-filled tunnel wearing a hood he had invented, and brought men out alive. Then the national news left him out.
sections: Paris, Kentucky, to Cleveland

Garrett Morgan was born in Paris, Kentucky, on 4 March 1877, to Sydney and Eliza Morgan, both formerly enslaved. He had six years of schooling. At fourteen he left for Cincinnati, where he worked and paid a tutor out of his wages to keep learning. In June 1895 he moved to Cleveland and took a job sweeping floors at a dry-goods factory for five dollars a week.

He taught himself sewing machines, became an adjuster for clothing makers, and in 1907 opened his own shop repairing and selling them. By 1909 he had a tailoring shop with 32 employees. In 1908 he married Mary Hasek, a Czech immigrant; they had three sons. A liquid he had been testing to stop sewing needles scorching cloth turned out to straighten hair, and in 1913 he organised the G. A. Morgan Hair Refining Company to sell it.
The safety hood

In 1912 Morgan introduced a breathing device, a hood that let the wearer breathe in smoke and gas, and in 1914 he patented it. It won first prize at a safety exposition in New York that year, and a fire chief in Yonkers ordered six. Selling it was harder than inventing it. Because of prejudice against a Black inventor, he used a white salesman for demonstrations, and the Patent Office's own history says he sometimes presented himself as "George Mason", a Native American assistant. Among our sources, only the Patent Office tells that story.
Under Lake Erie, July 1916

On 24 July 1916 an explosion hit a waterworks tunnel being dug under Lake Erie, about four miles out from Cleveland, and natural gas filled it. A work crew was trapped. Two rescue parties went in and died in the gas. Early on 25 July the police called Morgan. He and his brother Frank arrived with about twenty hoods, and Morgan led the third rescue party into the tunnel. They brought out survivors and recovered bodies. The disaster killed twenty people.
Sources disagree on how many were rescued alive: the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History records two rescued, the Patent Office eight. No number is claimed here.
Left out of the story

Morgan received bravery medals from a Cleveland civic association and from the International Association of Fire Engineers. But he was denied the money other rescuers received, the city would not support his nomination for a Carnegie Hero medal while four white rescuers got theirs, and his part was left out of the national news. Some Southern cities cancelled orders for the hood when they learned the inventor was Black. The Black press told the story; the Cleveland mayor was reluctant to honour him in public. In 1918, with the United States at war, the Navy ordered hoods for its warships.
The traffic signal

After seeing a collision at an intersection, Morgan patented a traffic signal on 20 November 1923: a hand-cranked post with movable arms and, between stop and go, a caution position that halted traffic in every direction. He demonstrated it in Willoughby, Ohio, and sold the rights to General Electric for 40,000 dollars. He is often credited with inventing the traffic light; he did not, and the signal itself was not widely used, but its caution step is the idea behind today's yellow light.

Morgan went on to found the weekly Cleveland Call in 1920, helped found the Cleveland Association of Colored Men, bought a farm near Wakeman and opened a country club there for Black Clevelanders, and received his last patent, for a comb, in 1956. He died in Cleveland on 27 July 1963 and is buried in Lake View Cemetery.
